newsitem.title: UK: London commodity markets welcome regulator accord.
newsitem.headline: London commodity markets welcome regulator accord.

text.p: Officials at commodity exchanges welcomed an agreement reached Tuesday by global regulators to strengthen supervision in commodity markets.
"We are in favour of increased co-operation, as good regulation is good for business," Lynton Jones, Chief Executive of the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) said.

"We welcome this initiative by the SIB, CFTC, MITI, and MAFF, which recognizes the benefits of enhanced co-operation and regulation," David King, Chief Executive of the London Metal Exchange (LME) said.
The IPE is Europe's leading energy market, trading crude oil and gas oil, while the LME is the world's largest non-ferrous metals market, trading metals such as copper and aluminium.
The London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE), which also trades a range of agricultural products ranging from coffee to wheat, was unable to comment.

Earlier this week regulators from 17 countries met in London, agreeing a range of measures enhancing standards and best practice in contract design, market surveillance and information-sharing and cooperation.

Representatives from many other commodity producing countries also attended the talks, which were co-hosted by the UK's Securities and Investment Board (SIB), the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI).
No new measures were agreed at the meeting, but the regulators decided to utilise their current regulatory powers.
Jones said there was a need to ensure that professional markets do not become over-regulated.
But he favoured measures which address regulatory differences between countries with similar contracts -- the IPE has an offset agreement with Singapore's SIMEX, he said.
"We need to have a level playing field, and these talks will lead to this," he said.

King said that the commodity agreement built on the basic principle of enhanced cooperation, although it had to be recognized that in some jurisdictions there were regulatory restraints on how much information could be released.
Information-sharing on large positions was already established between international regulators, following the 1995 Windsor Meeting which focused on financial markets.
Under separate pacts reached at a meeting in Boca Raton, 55 exchanges share confidential information on large positions, with umbrella agreements also covering 15 regulatory bodies.
